title: Ultra-processed food consumption and exposure to phthalates and bisphenols in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2013–2014
authors: Buckley JP, Kim H, Wong E, Rebholz CM
population: NHANES 2013–2014 participants aged 6 years or older with a 24-hour dietary recall and spot urine measurements
funder: This study was supported by grant funding from the National Institutes of Health (JPB: P30 DK072488, R01 ES030078; CMR: K01 DK107782, R21 HL143089). The findings and conclusions in this manuscript are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the National Institutes of Health.
authorConflicts: The authors declare they have no actual or potential competing financial interests.
result: Each 10% higher share of energy from ultra-processed food was associated with 8.0% (95% CI 5.6% to 10.3%) higher creatinine-standardised urinary mono-(carboxyisoctyl) phthalate (MCOP), a metabolite of the DEHP substitute diisononyl phthalate (17% in children, 5% in adolescents, 9% in adults), and with higher MCPP and MCNP; no association with MBzP, the sum of four DEHP metabolites, or bisphenols A, F and S. Higher energy from minimally processed food was associated with lower MCPP, MCNP, MCOP and bisphenols A and F.
